finding.claim: Mass assignment: PUT /me copies the entire request body onto the authenticated user object and saves it. Any user can set privileged or protected fields such as role, isAdmin, id, email verification status, or tenant/org id, which allows privilege escalation or account takeover.
finding.source: req.body (JSON) on PUT /me, controlled by any authenticated low-privilege user

trace.note: PUT /me handler; the only auth is whatever upstream middleware populates req.user, and no field allowlist is applied
Object.assign merges all attacker-supplied keys into req.user
The mutated user is persisted via req.store.save, so the escalated fields are stored
The modified user is returned in the response

finding.guards_checked: No allowlist, schema validation, or field filtering in this file. Only one file exists in the repo, so I could not see upstream middleware. The sibling route PUT /me/profile at users.js:11-12 destructures only displayName and bio, which shows the intended allowlist is missing from /me. Object.assign does not set __proto__ as a prototype, so prototype pollution is not claimed.

verdict.reason: users.js:5 does Object.assign(req.user, req.body) with no allowlist or validation, users.js:6 persists it and users.js:7 returns it, while the sibling route at users.js:11-12 shows the intended allowlist; upstream auth middleware isn't in the repo but any authenticated user reaches this, and the claimed fields (role, isAdmin, etc.) are a plausible impact though the file doesn't define the user schema.
